AI Verification: Proving Neural Network Robustness

This script demonstrates how to verify that neural networks behave correctly using formal methods from the AI Verification Library. At the edge, mistakes are expensive -- once an AI model is optimized, compiled, and connected to real sensors, failures are harder to diagnose. Formal verification provides mathematical guarantees about model behavior that go beyond what testing alone can achieve.
The script covers three progressively more rigorous approaches using the ACAS Xu (Airborne Collision Avoidance System for unmanned aircraft) neural networks:
  1. Explore the network -- understand what the ACAS Xu system does, how its neural networks make predictions, and observe advisory transitions as aircraft separation changes.
  2. Verify local robustness -- use the CROWN and α-CROWN algorithms to formally prove (or disprove) that the network's advisory is stable under bounded input perturbations at a single operating point.
  3. Verify global stability via adaptive mesh -- scale verification across the entire operational design domain, producing a verification map and quantifying how much of the input space is formally proven stable.
Based on the example Verify and Deploy ACAS Xu Neural Networks.

Setup

Verify that the required toolboxes and add-ons are installed, and prepare the models. If this is your first time running the exercise, run helper.setupModels to download the ACAS Xu neural networks.
if ~isfolder("model"), mkdir("models"), end;
if isempty(dir(fullfile("models", "*.mat")))
addpath("models")
helper.setupModels;
end

Stage 1: Explore ACAS Xu Neural Networks

ACAS Xu (Airborne Collision Avoidance System for unmanned aircraft) uses neural networks to recommend steering advisories that prevent mid-air collisions. The original system used a numeric lookup table requiring ~2 GB of storage. By replacing each table with a small neural network, the full system fits in ~3 MB -- a critical advantage for resource-constrained unmanned platforms.
The system comprises 45 neural networks, one for each combination of previous advisory (5 values) and discretized time-until-loss-of-vertical-separation τ (9 values).
  • : Time until loss of vertical separation (seconds). Values: [0, 1, 5, 10, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100]
  • : Previous advisory. Values: [Clear-of-Conflict, Weak Left, Weak Right, Strong Left, Strong Right]
Each network takes 5 inputs describing the positions and velocities of the ownship and intruder ship:
  • ρ : Distance from ownship to intruder (feet). Range/Values: [0, 60760]
  • : Angle to intruder relative to ownship heading direction, counterclockwise (radians). Range/Values: [, π]
  • ψ: Heading angle of intruder relative to ownship heading direction, counterclockwise (radians). Range/Values: [, π]
  • : Speed of ownship (ft/s). Range/Values: [100, 1200]
  • : Speed of intruder (ft/s). Range/Values: [0, 1200]
The network outputs scores for 5 advisories: Clear-of-Conflict (no action needed), Weak Left/Right (gentle turn), or Strong Left/Right (urgent maneuver). The advisory with the highest score is selected.

Load the ACAS Xu Network

Load the network for previous advisory = 1 (Clear-of-Conflict) and (imminent collision). This is one of 45 networks in the ACAS Xu system.
previousAdvisory = 1;
tau = 1;
acasNet = helper.loadACASNetwork(previousAdvisory, tau);
 
advisoryNames = helper.classNames;
disp("Advisory classes: " + join(string(advisoryNames), ", "))
Advisory classes: Clear-of-Conflict, Weak Left, Weak Right, Strong Left, Strong Right

Predict an Advisory

"Left Abeam" scenario:
Consider the "Left Abeam" scenario: two aircraft separated by 15,000 ft, with the intruder directly to the left (). The ownship flies at 954.6 ft/s and the intruder at 1050 ft/s with a slight relative heading offset ( rad). Predict the advisory at this single operating point.
rho0 = 15000;
theta = pi/2;
psi = -0.4296;
vOwn = 954.6;
vInt = 1050;
 
X0 = dlarray([rho0 theta psi vOwn vInt], "BC");
scores = predict(acasNet, X0);
nominalLabel = scores2label(scores, advisoryNames)
nominalLabel = categorical
Weak Right
The network recommends Weak Right -- a gentle turn away from the intruder. But what happens as the aircraft get closer?

Simulate an Encounter Trajectory

Simulate 100 seconds of straight-line flight (open-loop -- both aircraft maintain heading regardless of advisory). As time progresses, the horizontal separation decreases. At each timestep, query the network for its recommended advisory and observe how the advisory changes as the collision threat evolves.
t = (0:99)';
numSteps = numel(t);
 
% Ownship trajectory (flying north along y-axis)
xOwn = zeros(numSteps, 1);
yOwn = vOwn * t;
 
% Intruder trajectory (starting at the Left Abeam position)
xInt0 = rho0 * sin(theta);
yInt0 = rho0 * cos(theta);
xInt = xInt0 + vInt * sin(-psi) * t;
yInt = yInt0 + vInt * cos(-psi) * t;
 
% Compute separation at each timestep
rhoTraj = sqrt((xInt - xOwn).^2 + (yInt - yOwn).^2);
 
% Predict advisory at each timestep
XTraj = repmat([rho0, theta, psi, vOwn, vInt], [numSteps, 1]);
XTraj(:,1) = rhoTraj;
YTraj = predict(acasNet, dlarray(XTraj, "BC"));
advisoryTraj = scores2label(YTraj, advisoryNames);

Visualize Advisory Transitions

Plot the horizontal separation and the network's advisory over time. As the aircraft converge, the advisory transitions from Clear-of-Conflict to increasingly urgent maneuver recommendations. These transitions define the decision boundaries of the network -- the regions in input space where the advisory changes.
figure
tiledlayout(2,1)
 
nexttile
plot(t, rhoTraj, LineWidth=1.5)
ylabel("Separation \rho (ft)")
title("Encounter Trajectory — Left Abeam Configuration")
grid on
 
nexttile
advisoryIdx = double(advisoryTraj);
scatter(t, advisoryIdx, 20, advisoryIdx, "filled")
yticks(1:5)
yticklabels(string(advisoryNames))
ylim([0.5 5.5])
xlabel("Time (s)")
ylabel("Advisory")
title("Network Advisory Over Time")
colormap(helper.getClassColormapMatrix)
grid on
The network transitions between advisories as the encounter evolves -- from Clear-of-Conflict when the aircraft are far apart, to progressively more urgent maneuvers as separation decreases. These advisory transitions are the decision boundaries that formal verification will analyze.
But how confident can we be in these transitions? Testing individual points tells us what the network predicts at those points, but says nothing about what happens between them. A small change in velocity or angle might push the network to a different advisory. Formal verification answers this question with mathematical certainty.

Stage 2: Verify Local Robustness

Instead of testing individual inputs, formal verification proves that every input within a bounded region produces the same output. The verifyNetworkRobustness function uses the CROWN algorithm to compute an overapproximation of the network's reachable output set and determines whether the predicted class is guaranteed to dominate.
The verifyNetworkRobustness function checks whether the network classifies all outputs for a given input range as the same class. The function has three possible outputs:
  • verified — The network is robust to adversarial inputs between the specified bounds.
  • violated — The network is not robust to adversarial inputs between the specified bounds.
  • unproven — The function is unable to prove whether the network is robust to adversarial inputs between the specified bounds.

Define the Operating Point

Return to the Left Abeam scenario at the original separation of 15,000 ft. The expected advisory is Weak Right (class 3).
X = [15000 pi/2 -0.4296 954.6 1050];
label = 3; % Weak Right

Small Perturbation: Verified

Allow the velocity inputs (features 4 and 5) to vary by while keeping geometric inputs fixed. With this small perturbation, the verifier should return "verified", formally proving the network is robust -- every input in this region produces the same advisory.
dX = 0.03;
xLower = X .* [1 1 1 1-dX 1-dX];
xUpper = X .* [1 1 1 1+dX 1+dX];
 
xLower = dlarray(xLower, "BC");
xUpper = dlarray(xUpper, "BC");
 
result = verifyNetworkRobustness(acasNet, xLower, xUpper, label) %#ok<*NASGU>
result = categorical
verified

Larger Perturbation: Unproven

Increase the velocity perturbation to . With a wider input range, the CROWN algorithm's overapproximation of nonlinear (ReLU) layers may produce output bounds that are too loose to separate the correct class from all others. An "unproven" result does not mean the network is wrong -- it means the algorithm cannot determine the answer with the current precision.
dX = 0.08;
xLower = dlarray(X .* [1 1 1 1-dX 1-dX], "BC");
xUpper = dlarray(X .* [1 1 1 1+dX 1+dX], "BC");
 
[result, detailedResult] = verifyNetworkRobustness(acasNet, xLower, xUpper, label) %#ok<*ASGLU>
result = categorical
unproven
detailedResult = 1×5 categorical array
unproven verified <undefined> verified unproven
For the classes Weak Left and Strong Left, the function returns verified. This means that the network does not predict either of these classes anywhere within the input bounds. This makes sense, since the expected outcome is for the advisory to tell the aircraft to turn right.

Refine Verification by Partitioning Input Region

To reduce the amount of overapproximation of the output bounds, split the input region spanned by XLower and XUpper into several smaller input regions, then attempt to verify the network robustness on each of the subregions.
The figure shows how bisecting the input region can tighten the output bounds.
Bisect the region along the range of [966 1134] into [966 1050] and [1050 1134].
xLower = repmat(xLower,1,2);
xUpper = repmat(xUpper,1,2);
 
xLower(5,2) = 1050;
xUpper(5,1) = 1050;
label = [3 3];
Verify the robustness of these two subregions.
verifyNetworkRobustness(acasNet,xLower,xUpper,label)
ans = 2×1 categorical array
verified
verified

Refine with the α-CROWN Algorithm

The α-CROWN variant fine-tunes polyhedral constraints at ReLU layers to produce tighter output bounds at the cost of longer computation. Re-run verification on the full bounds (without partitioning) using Algorithm="alpha-crown".
dX = 0.08;
xLower = dlarray(X .* [1 1 1 1-dX 1-dX], "BC");
xUpper = dlarray(X .* [1 1 1 1+dX 1+dX], "BC");
label = 3;
resultAlpha = verifyNetworkRobustness(acasNet, xLower, xUpper, label, Algorithm="alpha-crown")
resultAlpha = categorical
verified

Compare Output Bounds: CROWN vs. α-CROWN

The estimateNetworkOutputBounds function computes the lower and upper bound of the output values that a network returns when the input is between specified input lower and upper bounds.
Visualize the output score bounds from both algorithms side-by-side. The α-CROWN bounds (red) are noticeably tighter than the CROWN bounds (blue). For CROWN, the bounds for Weak Right may overlap with other classes, preventing proof. For α-CROWN, there is no overlap.
[YLowerCROWN, YUpperCROWN] = estimateNetworkOutputBounds(acasNet, xLower, xUpper);
[YLowerAlpha, YUpperAlpha] = estimateNetworkOutputBounds(acasNet, xLower, xUpper, Algorithm="alpha-crown");
 
helper.displayBoundComparison(YLowerCROWN, YUpperCROWN, YLowerAlpha, YUpperAlpha)

A Genuinely Non-Robust Case

Increase the velocity perturbation to . At this scale, the input range covers physically different scenarios -- a very slow intruder may not pose a collision threat, causing the network to legitimately change its advisory. Neither algorithm can verify robustness.
dX = 0.25;
label = 3;
xLower = dlarray(X .* [1 1 1 1-dX 1-dX], "BC");
xUpper = dlarray(X .* [1 1 1 1+dX 1+dX], "BC");
xUpper(4:5) = min(xUpper(4:5), 1200);
 
[result, detailedResult] = verifyNetworkRobustness(acasNet, xLower, xUpper, label, Algorithm="alpha-crown")
result = categorical
unproven
detailedResult = 1×5 categorical array
unproven unproven <undefined> unproven unproven
The function returns unproven for all classes.
To prove that the network is not robust within this large input range, find an example input for which the network does not advise Weak Right by using the findAdversarialExamples function. The findAdversarialExamples finds adversarial examples starting from a random guess. Run the function repeatedly, up to 100 times or until it finds an adversarial example.
for ii = 1:100
[xAdversarial,mislabel,iX] = findAdversarialExamples(acasNet,xLower,xUpper,label);
if ~isempty(xAdversarial)
disp("Adversial example found after " + ii + " attempts.")
disp(mat2str(extractdata(xAdversarial)',4))
advisory = helper.classNames(mislabel)
break
end
end
Adversial example found after 33 attempts.
[1.5e+04 1.571 -0.4296 1181 811.1]
advisory = categorical
Clear-of-Conflict

Stage 3: Verify Global Stability Using Adaptive Mesh

In Stage 2, you verified robustness at a single operating point. But safety-critical systems must be verified across their entire operational envelope. A uniform grid approach wastes computation: most of the input space is far from decision boundaries and verifies easily, while boundary regions need fine resolution.
The adaptive mesh algorithm starts with the entire operational design domain (ODD) as one hypercuboid. If verification succeeds, the region is marked stable. If unproven, the hypercuboid is bisected along its widest angular dimension and each half is re-verified. This continues until all regions are verified or the minimum resolution is reached.

Configure the Operational Design Domain

Fix the distance ( ft) and velocities ( ft/s, ft/s) while sweeping the two heading angles (θ and ψ) across the full range . The minAngle parameter (in radians) prevents infinite subdivision. Larger miniBatchSize values use GPU memory more efficiently.
minAngle = 0.01;
miniBatchSize = 4096;
 
rho = 15000;
 
thetaLower = -pi;
thetaUpper = pi;
psiLower = -pi;
psiUpper = pi;
 
oddLower = [rho thetaLower psiLower vOwn vInt];
oddUpper = [rho thetaUpper psiUpper vOwn vInt];

Initialize Data Structures

Create the initial hypercuboid spanning the entire ODD, a queue for processing, and storage for verified results. The helper.CubeBatch class holds collections of hypercuboids and the helper.CubeBatchQueue manages the FIFO processing queue.
oddLower = dlarray(oddLower, "BC");
oddUpper = dlarray(oddUpper, "BC");
 
cubes = helper.CubeBatch(oddLower, oddUpper);
verifiedCubes = helper.CubeBatch;
cubeQueue = helper.CubeBatchQueue;
enqueue(cubeQueue, cubes);
 
numHypercuboids = 0;
verifiedLabelBatch = [];
hypercuboidCenters = [];
helper.adaptiveMeshProgressMonitor;

Run the Adaptive Mesh Verification Loop

The main loop repeatedly: (1) retrieves a batch of hypercuboids from the queue, (2) predicts the advisory at each center, (3) calls verifyNetworkRobustness to check if the predicted advisory holds across the entire region, (4) stores verified regions and bisects unproven ones.
Watch the figure update in real time. Colored rectangles represent verified regions, with each color corresponding to an advisory class. The algorithm concentrates subdivisions near decision boundaries. With minAngle=0.1, this should complete in 1-3 minutes.
while ~isempty(cubeQueue)
cubes = getCubes(cubeQueue, miniBatchSize);
 
centers = getCenters(cubes);
hypercuboidCenters = [hypercuboidCenters extractdata(centers)]; %#ok<AGROW>
 
advisory = predict(acasNet, centers);
[~, idxLabel] = max(extractdata(advisory));
 
results = verifyNetworkRobustness(acasNet, cubes.xLower, cubes.xUpper, idxLabel, MiniBatchSize=miniBatchSize);
idxVerified = (results == "verified");
idxUnproven = (results == "unproven");
 
verifiedMiniBatch = getSubset(cubes, idxVerified);
verifiedLabel = idxLabel(idxVerified);
verifiedLabelBatch = [verifiedLabelBatch verifiedLabel]; %#ok<AGROW>
verifiedCubes = addSubset(verifiedCubes, verifiedMiniBatch);
 
xlVerified = extractdata(verifiedMiniBatch.xLower);
xuVerified = extractdata(verifiedMiniBatch.xUpper);
sideLengths = xuVerified - xlVerified;
for kk = 1:getNumCubes(verifiedMiniBatch)
hold on
rectangle( ...
Position=[xlVerified(2,kk) xlVerified(3,kk) sideLengths(2,kk) sideLengths(3,kk)], ...
FaceColor=[helper.getClassColors(verifiedLabel(kk)) 0.05], ...
EdgeColor="none");
end
hold off
drawnow
 
unprovenCubes = getSubset(cubes, idxUnproven);
helper.bisectAndUpdateQueue(cubeQueue, unprovenCubes, minAngle);
 
numHypercuboids = numHypercuboids + getNumCubes(cubes);
end

Analyze Sample Points

Verify that the network predictions at specific sample points match the verified regions in the plot. Each sample point should produce an advisory that matches the color of the region it falls in.
samplePoints = [
[rho -3.00 3.00 vOwn vInt]; % Clear-of-Conflict
[rho -1.50 1.00 vOwn vInt]; % Strong Left
[rho -0.78 2.10 vOwn vInt]; % Weak Left
[rho -0.78 1.57 vOwn vInt]; % Strong Right
[rho -0.39 1.97 vOwn vInt]; % Weak Right
[rho 0.70 -1.57 vOwn vInt]; % Strong Left
[rho 0.78 -0.78 vOwn vInt]; % Weak Left
[rho 0.90 -1.57 vOwn vInt]; % Strong Right
[rho 1.57 -0.78 vOwn vInt]; % Weak Right
[rho 0.95 -1.97 vOwn vInt]; % Strong Right
];
 
advisory = predict(acasNet, samplePoints);
sampleAdvisory = scores2label(advisory, advisoryNames)
sampleAdvisory = 10×1 categorical array

The class labels in each region match those from the global stability analysis.

Compute Verification Coverage

Calculate what fraction of the ODD was formally verified as stable. With minAngle=0.1, a high proportion of the ODD should be verified (typically >90%). The unverified regions concentrate at decision boundaries.
totalVolume = prod(oddUpper(2:3) - oddLower(2:3));
verifiedVolume = sum(prod(verifiedCubes.xUpper(2:3,:) - verifiedCubes.xLower(2:3,:)));
 
disp("Stable proportion of ODD: " + extractdata(verifiedVolume / totalVolume));
Stable proportion of ODD: 0.9901
disp("Number of hypercuboids: " + numHypercuboids);
Number of hypercuboids: 53973

Visualize Class Proportions

Plot a bar chart showing how much of the ODD belongs to each advisory class, plus the unverified fraction. Clear-of-Conflict typically dominates the ODD. The unverified fraction is small and corresponds to decision boundaries.
helper.plotClassProportion(verifiedLabelBatch, verifiedCubes, totalVolume)

Visualize Hypercuboid Density

Plot a 2D histogram of hypercuboid center locations. Dense clusters indicate where the algorithm performed the most subdivisions -- high density along decision boundaries, low density in the stable interior of each advisory region.
helper.plotHypercuboidDensity(hypercuboidCenters)

Summary

This exercise demonstrated three progressively rigorous approaches to AI verification, all using the ACAS Xu collision avoidance system:
  1. Exploration revealed that the network transitions between advisories as encounter geometry changes. These decision boundaries are the critical regions where verification matters most.
  2. Local robustness verification used formal methods (CROWN and α-CROWN) to provide mathematical guarantees about network behavior within bounded input regions. The three possible outcomes -- verified, unproven, and violated -- give precise information about robustness and the effectiveness of different algorithms.
  3. Adaptive mesh verification scaled formal methods to the entire operational design domain. The algorithm concentrates computation on decision boundaries while quickly verifying stable interior regions, achieving high coverage efficiently.
Try this: Re-run the adaptive mesh loop with minAngle = 0.05 for higher resolution. How does the verified proportion change? How many more hypercuboids are processed
